# Clearing the air: microcosting the carbon impact of drug-susceptible pulmonary TB treatment

**Authors:** M.F. Martins; M.R. Dauphinais; A. Tabackman; P.B. Narasimhan; M.C. Nielsen; N.S. Miller; A. Sahay; M. Namachivayam; S Janarthanan; C. Palanivel; S. Lakshminarayanan; K.G. Koura; P. Sinha

**Affiliations:** 1Boston Medical Center, Boston, MA, USA | 2Boston University School of Medicine, Boston, MA, USA | 3Jawaharlal Institute for Postgraduate Medical Education and Research, Puducherry, India | 4Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore, MD, USA | 5International Union Against Tuberculosis and Lung Disease, Paris, France | 6UMR261 MERIT, Université Paris Cité, IRD, F-75006, Paris, France

## Abstract

More than 10 million individuals develop active TB each year. The diagnosis and treatment of TB create greenhouse gas emissions, contributing to climate change. This study estimates the carbon footprint (CF) of successfully treating one person with drug-susceptible pulmonary TB (DS-PTB) in India.

We defined the cascade of care for DS-PTB using national guidelines, interviews, and direct observation. We estimated the inputs for TB diagnosis and treatment in United States dollars, kilowatts per hour, and kilometres travelled; we converted them into carbon dioxide emissions equivalents (CO2e) using an appropriate calculator.

The CF of diagnosing and treating one person with DS-PTB in India is 103.8 kg CO2e: 31.9% attributable to diagnosis and 68.1% to treatment. Emissions came primarily from first-line drugs (21.2%), hospitalisations (17.4%), and laboratory processes.

We conservatively estimate that treating all persons with TB in India would produce at least 290,640 metric tonnes of CO2e per year, approximately the same emissions as 63,182 passenger cars in the United States. It is evident that one of India’s leading public health challenges also contributes meaningfully to climate change.

TB has been the leading cause of death from a single infectious agent for years, only surpassed by COVID-19 during the recent pandemic.1 In 2022, an estimated 10.6 million people fell ill with TB worldwide.1 India accounted for 27% of those cases, with the highest number of TB cases.1 In 2022, an estimated 2.8 million Indians developed TB, 75% of whom had pulmonary TB.2 The treatment success rate for TB in India is approximately 87%.

The processes involved in TB diagnosis and treatment require significant material and energy input, which produce greenhouse gases (GHG), directly contributing to climate change.3,4 GHG emissions add to the pre-existing stock of carbon in the atmosphere, exacerbating global warming, changes in rainfall, sea level rise, increased intensity of hurricanes, and ocean acidification.5 A CF is the estimation of the direct and indirect GHG emissions associated with a sector, process, or product,6 which is measured in carbon dioxide equivalents (CO2e).

Climate change is a threat to all species, and there is growing interest in how it affects human health and disease patterns.7 Ironically, the healthcare sector itself is responsible for an estimated 5% of all global carbon emissions.8 The CO2 emissions related to healthcare come from the global supply chain of goods and services purchased by medical retail, hospitals, and ambulatory healthcare services, including heating, water and electricity generation, transport, pharmaceutical, and chemical products.8

Various authors have already raised the need to estimate the CF of TB as a powerful tool to justify the urge to invest in preventive measures and guide policies towards less carbon-intensive healthcare systems.3,4 This study aims to estimate the marginal CF of successfully treating one patient with drug-susceptible pulmonary TB (DS-PTB) in India to raise awareness of its environmental impact.

## METHODS

We estimated the CF of DS-PTB, as this is the most common manifestation of TB and has the most uniform diagnosis and treatment. To do this, we first defined the cascade of care for DS-PTB based on the National Strategic Plan for TB Elimination,9,10 the WHO Standards for TB Care in India,11 interviews with key informants, and direct observation during visits to a district TB centre (DTC) in Tamil Nadu, India. The key informants were members of our team who work in Puducherry and Tamil Nadu, including doctors and social workers engaged deeply in TB research in India.

We classified the cascade of care processes into diagnosis and treatment. Ethics approval or informed consent was not required as the investigation did not involve human subjects.

We used a bottom-up approach to identify carbon costs. To do so, we visited a DTC and enquired about the treatment and triage algorithms, duration of hospitalisations, frequency of contact, and the distances travelled by persons with TB disease (PWTB). We also observed procedures of specimen collection, processing, and testing. We inventoried fixed and consumable items used in the diagnosis and treatment of TB and enquired about their costs. When we could not obtain the costs directly through observation, we obtained quantitative data from published literature,12-14 and websites for similar equipment.15-20 We measured each variable in United States dollars (USD) for costs, kilowatts per hour (kWh) for electricity, and kilometres (km) for distance.

Subsequently, we converted these inputs into CO2e with the Carbon Footprint Ltd (Basingstoke, UK) calculator, available online.21 In this calculator, we used the following categories: pharmaceuticals (USD), electricity (kWh), and distance travelled by bus (km). Since the calculator did not have a specific category for diagnostic tests, when assessing sputum smear microscopy and nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT), we chose the category of pharmaceuticals, which we deemed the nearest option.

## RESULTS

### Care cascade

The process begins when an individual presents to a healthcare facility with respiratory symptoms and is prescribed antibiotic therapy for 2–3 days. If symptoms fail to improve, the individual is referred to a primary health centre (PHC) or a DTC, where a chest X-ray is performed and two sputum samples are collected. Approximately 5–10% of individuals need to be hospitalised due to the severity of the symptoms, with a typical minimum length of hospitalisation spanning seven days.

Afterwards, sputum samples are processed in a Biosafety Level 3 (BSL3) laboratory for sputum smear, mycobacterial culture, and NAAT. The machinery required for this includes heating, ventilation, and air conditioning (HVAC), a biosafety cabinet, an automated broth culture system, a freezer, and an autoclave, all of which require significant energy input. PWTB was treated in the ambulatory setting and returned to the DTC 2 days later. They have blood tests performed (complete blood count, glycaemia, kidney function, liver function, and HIV antigen/antibody screen), are registered in the electronic database of TB cases in India (Nikshay), and are provided with the first month's supply of TB therapy: 2RHZE/4RHE (2 months of daily rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol, followed by 4 months of daily rifampicin, isoniazid and ethambutol).

PWTB attend monthly appointments at the PHC, except for Months 2 and 6 of treatment (the end of the initiation and maintenance phases, respectively) when they go to the DTC for blood tests and two sputum samples collected each time for smear microscopy and culture. At Month 2, most patients are able to produce a sputum sample, but this is reduced to 50% by Month 6 (Figure 1).

### Carbon costs of diagnosing and fully treating one person with DS-PTB in India

Diagnosis included initial empiric antibiotics (USD1.83), one chest radiograph (0.76 kg CO2e), two sputum smear microscopies (USD6.54), one NAAT (USD23.59), two sputum cultures (2.11 kWh), electricity usage of two outpatient visits (1.03 kWh), patient transportation to those visits (32 km by bus with 50 people), and BSL3 laboratory appliances: HVAC and biosafety cabinet (10.11 kWh), freezer (1.14 kWh), autoclave (12.5 kWh), and lighting (0.13 kWh). Treatment accounted for costs of first-line drugs for DS-PTB (USD54.0), four sputum smear microscopies (USD9.79) and four sputum cultures (3.17 kWh), as well as electricity usage of seven outpatient visits (3.61 kWh), patient transportation to those visits (334 km by bus with 50 people), and inpatient bed days if required (25.33 kWh).

We followed a conservative approach, limiting our estimates to the main processes involved in each step, excluding smaller collateral processes (e.g., blood tests). We also considered only marginal costs for each variable, disregarding fixed costs. We estimated the CF of diagnosing and treating one person with DS-PTB in India to be 103.8 kg CO2e: 31.9% attributable to diagnosis and 68.1% to treatment. Regarding diagnosis, the variables that accounted for most of the CO2e were NAAT (9.3%), as well as some laboratory machines: autoclave (8.6%) and HVAC and biosafety cabinet (7.0%). Respectively, in the treatment category, the largest variables were first-line drugs (21.2%) and hospitalisations (17.4%), followed by the same laboratory machines: autoclave, HVAC and biosafety cabinet (Table and Figure 2).

Because we assumed all patients travelled to their appointments by bus, the CF attributable to transportation was very low (0.747 Kg CO2e). However, if all patients had travelled by car or motorcycle, this would have been much higher: 56.83 and 30.45 kg CO2e, respectively.

## DISCUSSION

To our knowledge, this analysis is the first one that has attempted to quantify the CF of TB treatment. Assuming all estimated 2.8 million PWTB cases with an incidence disease in 2022 were fully treated, the CF would have been at least 290,640 metric tonnes of CO2e.22 Despite conservative assumptions, the CF of treating PWTB in India per year is similar to the CO2e of 63,182 average passenger cars in the same time frame and more than all the minimally invasive surgeries in the United States each year.23

Because we only measured the processes related to DS-PTB and then extrapolated them to all types of TB, our results likely underestimated the country-level CF. The processes involved in the management of extrapulmonary TB (EPTB) and drug-resistant TB (DR-TB) were not included in the analysis. These are more complex, less standardised, and can involve longer treatment courses. Because of these reasons, the diagnosis and treatment of EP-TB and DR-TB carry higher costs14,22 and, thus, likely higher carbon costs too. More research is needed to define the carbon costs for EPTB and DR-TB.

Healthcare delivery in most countries is the largest service sector in terms of CF, comparable in size to the food sector.8,24 Pichler et al. conducted a cross-country comparison of the healthcare-related CF of 36 countries, where China was found to have the largest CO2e, followed by the United States, Japan, and India, reflecting primarily the income level and population size of each country.8

Healthcare is running behind other sectors regarding sustainability policies, and it has a high potential to decarbonise itself.24 Mitigation strategies could involve developing more carbon-efficient treatment algorithms, using telemedicine, and avoiding unnecessary interventions. Furthermore, investments could be made in more carbon-efficient medical equipment, laboratory techniques, heating and cooling systems, air purification systems, and medical transportation vehicles. There is also the scope of reducing the carbon intensity of the production and packaging of drugs and medical devices. Finally, a systemic shift from curative to preventive and from hospital to ambulatory care would likely reduce the overall healthcare CF.8

Applying low-carbon strategies requires specialised knowledge about the carbon intensity of each source of emissions involved in the life cycle of healthcare delivery, the cost-effectiveness of different alternatives, and their potential impact on health outcomes.8,25 The main goal of healthcare delivery is to achieve the best health outcomes possible. Therefore, any decarbonising strategy should not compromise the quality of care. On the contrary, many of these interventions are likely to improve health outcomes both at system and individual levels. In this regard, the use of telemedicine or community health workers could be beneficial by preventing some of the PWTB’s travel, especially travel in private vehicles. Reductions in this aspect would likely have other benefits as well, like reductions of catastrophic costs for PWTB.14,26

Although the CF of preventive measures (e.g., vaccination, contact tracing) has not been measured, it is likely that investing in a primarily preventive approach against TB will be less carbon-intensive. Moreover, once we manage to end this long-lasting epidemic, all CF related to TB will have been eliminated.4 Additionally, as a large fraction of PWTB develops post-TB chronic lung disease and chronic disability, the carbon savings from TB prevention would extend far beyond just the reductions assessed in our analysis. These must be considered in policy analyses.25 As such, countries should focus on addressing social determinants of health, such as malnutrition, which would reduce TB incidence and general healthcare utilisation.27

The GHG emissions associated with TB will continue to be generated each year as long as this disease is not eradicated. There are multiple benefits of ending TB, both from an individual and community perspective, including reducing morbidity, mortality, and disability and, thus, the amount of healthcare services needed. If we add to this the contribution to the United Nations’ Sustainable Development Goal number 13 by reducing global CF, the argument to invest in TB eradication becomes even stronger.4,28

This analysis has numerous strengths. It is novel to apply a micro-costing strategy from traditional health economics to estimate the carbon costs of TB treatment. We have relied on direct observation of TB diagnostic and treatment processes to determine carbon costs rather than making top-down assessments. Additionally, we have not restricted ourselves to just healthcare costs but have also accounted for carbon costs accrued through transportation.

Limitations of this study include the lack of standardised methods to estimate CO2e accurately and the use of a calculator that is optimised neither for India nor for some of the variables considered. Additionally, we only measured the marginal costs for each process, excluding fixed costs, and disregarded some collateral consumables and processes, such as laboratory waste disposal. We did not include individuals who were evaluated for TB but tested negative, which occurs in approximately 90% of people who are tested for TB. Our CF estimate did not consider care for key TB comorbidities such as HIV, malnutrition, and diabetes, which are common and necessitate co-management during TB treatment. Finally, we based our estimate on the cascade of care followed within the state of Tamil Nadu, extrapolating to the rest of India, but the equipment, logistics and distances may vary from state to state. It is worth mentioning that the CO2e attributed to some variables like NAAT may be overestimated as it is directly proportional to the cost, but there is no further evidence to justify a higher carbon cost.

Further research is warranted to investigate the CF of TB in other countries, particularly under different socio-economic situations. Moreover, future lines of investigation should include GHG emissions of preventive measures and TB-related morbidity and disability. Additionally, methodological work is needed to develop suitable CF calculators to assess diagnostic and therapeutic methods to measure the CF of various healthcare interventions. Finally, our research highlights the need to identify other opportunities to promote sustainability in the healthcare sector as a whole.

Despite a conservative approach, the estimate of CF of TB in India was sizeable, indicating that one of India’s leading public health challenges also contributes meaningfully to climate change. In our pursuit of eradicating TB, we must integrate environmental sustainability into our strategies, ensuring we do not win the battle against TB only to lose the war for our planet's future.
